title: What makes a strong password? Length, entropy and NIST rules — cv.cm
description: Password strength comes from length and randomness, not symbol rules. Current NIST SP 800-63B guidance, entropy math with examples, and passphrases compared.
answer: A strong password is long, randomly generated and used for only one account. Length and randomness matter more than mixing symbols: NIST SP 800-63B now recommends at least 15 characters when a password is the only factor, no forced composition rules, no scheduled expiry, and checks against lists of breached passwords. Four random words from a 7,776-word list give about 51.7 bits of entropy; six give about 77.5 bits.

body: Attackers do not guess letter by letter. They try leaked passwords first, then dictionary words with common substitutions, then patterns such as a capitalized word followed by a year and `!`. A password like `P@ssw0rd2024!` satisfies most complexity rules and still falls early, because every part of it is predictable.

Entropy measures how many guesses a password needs when it was generated at random. For a password of length L picked uniformly from a set of N symbols, entropy is L × log2(N) bits, and each extra bit doubles the work. The formula only applies to random generation; it says nothing useful about a password a person made up.

Worked example: log2(7,776) = 12.925, so four random words give 4 × 12.925 ≈ 51.7 bits, about 3.7 × 10^15 possibilities. An attacker running 10 billion guesses per second against a leaked fast hash would cover them all in roughly 4 days. Six words take about 700,000 years at the same rate.

Online attacks are far slower, since login forms rate-limit and lock out. The large margins matter for offline attacks after a database leak, where the guess rate depends on how the site stored the hash.
NIST Special Publication 800-63B, revision 4, finalized in 2025, sets password rules for US federal systems and is widely copied elsewhere. Its main requirements for services that accept passwords:

ul: Minimum length of 15 characters when the password is the only authenticator, and 8 when it is part of multi-factor authentication.
Allow passwords of at least 64 characters, and accept spaces, all printable ASCII and Unicode characters.
No composition rules such as requiring a digit, an uppercase letter and a symbol.
No forced periodic changes. Require a change only when there is evidence of compromise.
Check new passwords against a blocklist of breached, common or context-specific values such as the service name or username.
No password hints or security questions, and allow paste so password managers work.

body: The reasoning is that composition rules and expiry push people toward predictable patterns like `Summer2025!` becoming `Autumn2025!`, which add little real entropy.

head: Random characters
Random words
rows: Accounts stored in a password manager
The few passwords you must memorize

body: Words must be picked at random, with dice or a generator, not chosen by you. A phrase from a song, a quote or a sentence you would write has far less entropy than its length suggests.

ol: Use a password manager and let it generate a unique random password, 16 characters or more, for every account. CISA gives the same advice.
Memorize only a few passphrases: the password manager's master password and your device login. Use five or six random words.
Never reuse a password. Credential stuffing, trying leaked email and password pairs on other sites, is one of the most common account takeovers.
Turn on multi-factor authentication, preferably passkeys or an authenticator app rather than SMS, for email, banking and the password manager.
Change a password when a service reports a breach, not on a calendar schedule.

body.note: Strength meters on websites estimate guessability from patterns and can disagree with each other. A generator that runs in your browser using the Web Crypto API produces passwords without sending them anywhere; avoid tools that generate passwords on a remote server.

faq.q: How long should a password be?
faq.a: At least 15 characters for an account protected only by a password, per NIST SP 800-63B rev 4. For randomly generated passwords stored in a manager, 16 to 20 characters is a comfortable default.

faq.q: Are passphrases more secure than passwords?
faq.a: They can be, if the words are chosen at random. Six random words beat a typical 10-character human-made password, but a 16-character random password has more entropy than six words.

faq.q: Should I change my passwords regularly?
faq.a: No. NIST advises against forced periodic changes because they lead to predictable variations. Change a password when there is a sign of compromise, such as a breach notice.

faq.q: Do special characters make a password stronger?
faq.a: Only slightly. Going from 62 to 94 possible characters adds about 0.6 bits per character, while adding one more character adds about 6.5 bits. Length helps more than symbols.
